title: A Hard Knobbly Liver and Weight Loss / Find the Primary, Start the Pathway

blocks.text: A Hard Knobbly Liver and Weight Loss / Find the Primary, Start the Pathway

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-16 · Physical examination · PACES Station 4, abdominal examination encounter · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 min: up to 6 min examining, then at least 4 min of examiner questions · Guidelines: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (published 23 June 2015; last updated 15 April 2026) · Related AMaC: Abdominal examination: chronic liver disease; splenomegaly

A 66-year-old man, a retired lorry driver, has lost weight over three months and feels full early. Please examine his abdomen and report what you find. You have up to 6 minutes to examine, followed by questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A hard, knobbly, non-tender liver with weight loss suggests liver metastases; the lesson is to look for the primary and start the suspected cancer pathway.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates say "hepatomegaly" and list causes, never describing the edge or searching for the primary. Pass: describe the edge, find the signs of spread, plan imaging and referral. Fail: stop at "big liver".

rows: Look at the whole man, then the liver.
"May I examine your tummy? Tell me if anything is sore."
Introduce, consent, ask about pain, expose; look for cachexia, jaundice, hands, nodes.
Describe the liver and search for the primary.
"I'm going to feel your tummy, starting away from any tender areas."
Liver edge, surface, size, tenderness; spleen, kidneys, masses, ascites; percuss, listen for a bruit.
Look for the primary and effects.
"May I check your neck and groins, and your legs?"
Left supraclavicular node, other nodes, ankles; request rectal examination, breast and chest check.
Give the diagnosis and the pathway.
"This is a hard irregular liver. I'm worried it's spread from another cancer."
Cover him, thank him; present findings, causes, plan.
Presses hard on the liver without asking; leaves him exposed
Introduces, obtains consent, cleans hands, asks about pain, palpates gently, covers him
Offers a chaperone and asks about his weight loss kindly
Starts at the liver; no percussion or search for ascites
Palpates from the right iliac fossa, percusses, checks spleen, kidneys and ascites
Listens for a bruit, checks nodes and requests rectal examination
Reports pulsatility or a bruit that is absent
Firm, irregular, non-tender liver edge several centimetres below the costal margin; cachexia; no ascites
States no jaundice, no splenomegaly, no supraclavicular node and no peripheral oedema
Liver metastases or primary liver cancer, with reasons from the edge and weight loss
Prioritises by the whole history and imaging: early satiety is non-specific; asks about bowel change, cough and a breast lump
Ultrasound or CT, liver tests, FBC, renal function and clotting; tumour markers only when directed by the suspected diagnosis and specialist team
Adds CT chest abdomen and pelvis when appropriate and specialist-team discussion; selective tumour markers, not a screening panel
Urgent investigation and suspected cancer pathway referral
Names the pathway, explains the next steps to him and gives a safety net

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice.
Not used for this station type: the patient is a real or simulated patient and the findings are in section 8.

Findings (released as each step is done). Thin, pale, muscle wasting. No jaundice. Firm, irregular, non-tender liver edge 6 cm below the costal margin (scenario). Spleen not palpable. No ascites; no bruit. No supraclavicular node; no oedema. Weight loss 8 kg in three months (scenario). Rectal examination, if requested: normal.

Question ladder. Q1 Findings and diagnosis (R3, R4): irregular hepatomegaly, probably liver metastases. Q2 Causes of irregular hepatomegaly (R4): metastases, hepatocellular carcinoma, polycystic liver. Q3 Primary (R5): colon, stomach, pancreas, lung, breast. Q4 Investigation (R6): imaging and baseline bloods; tumour markers selectively through the specialist team. Q5 Pathway (R7): NICE NG12 (1.2.11) advises considering an urgent direct access ultrasound scan to assess for liver cancer in people with an upper abdominal mass consistent with an enlarged liver; with a hard irregular liver and weight loss, cancer is suspected, so arrange urgent imaging and a suspected cancer pathway referral.
Normal-findings variant for a separate teaching exercise. Normal abdomen. The candidate must say the abdomen is normal. Do not switch the defined case to this variant during the encounter.
Curveball 1. "The liver is tender and pulsatile." Safe: consider tricuspid regurgitation or hepatic congestion.
Curveball 2. "Would you biopsy it now?" Safe: image first; the specialist team decides.
Curveball 3. "He is jaundiced." Safe: obstruction or extensive disease; urgent imaging.

Fail performance
(Presses hard on the liver without asking. [R1 Fail] Starts at the liver, no percussion. [R2 Fail])
CANDIDATE: There is a bruit and a pulsatile liver. [R3 Fail] It's cirrhosis. [R4 Fail] I can't say what primary. [R5 Fail]
EXAMINER: What next?
CANDIDATE: A biopsy first. [R6 Fail] See him in routine clinic. [R7 Fail]
Examiner note: Invented bruit, no primary and no pathway for a man with weight loss and an irregular liver.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello. May I examine your tummy? Tell me if it hurts. [R1 Pass]
(Palpates from the right iliac fossa, percusses, checks spleen, kidneys and ascites. [R2 Pass])
CANDIDATE: He is thin. The liver is firm, irregular and non-tender, several centimetres below the costal margin. No ascites or jaundice. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: This is probably liver metastases. [R4 Pass] The primary could be colon, stomach, pancreas, lung or breast. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: What next?

CANDIDATE: Ultrasound or CT, liver tests and other baseline bloods; AFP only if primary hepatocellular cancer is suspected. [R6 Pass] Urgent investigation and a suspected cancer pathway referral. [R7 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Thank you. I'll cover you. [R1 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and accurate. Did not search nodes or request rectal examination.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: Hello. May I examine your tummy? Tell me if it hurts. [R1 High]
(Palpates from the right iliac fossa, percusses, checks spleen, kidneys and ascites. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? Please say if you want me to stop. [R1 High]
(Listens for a bruit, checks the neck and groins for nodes, requests a rectal examination. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: Cachexia; a firm, irregular, non-tender liver edge 6 cm down; no jaundice, splenomegaly, ascites, node or oedema. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Metastases or primary liver cancer, given the knobbly edge and weight loss. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Early satiety may result from the enlarged liver or other disease; it does not identify a gastric primary; I'd ask about bowel change, cough and a breast lump. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: What next?
CANDIDATE: Appropriate CT staging and baseline bloods, with selective tumour markers and biopsy decisions through the specialist team. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: A suspected cancer pathway referral. I'd explain this to him and ask him to return with jaundice or pain. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: Thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 High]
Examiner note: Prioritised the primary by symptoms and explained the pathway.
R7: Routine review for weight loss and an irregular liver delays diagnosis.
R2: Starting at the liver edge can miss a markedly enlarged liver.
R3: Reporting a bruit that is absent suggests signs were assumed.
R4: Cirrhosis ignores the hard irregular edge and weight loss.
R5: Naming no primary leaves the search without direction.
"Let me describe the edge of the liver."
"I'd look for the primary."
"I'd refer on the suspected cancer pathway."
Firm irregular hepatomegaly: metastases, hepatocellular carcinoma, polycystic liver. Palpate from the right iliac fossa upwards.

NICE NG12 (published 23 June 2015; last updated 15 April 2026), recommendation 1.2.11: consider an urgent direct access ultrasound scan to assess for liver cancer in people with an upper abdominal mass consistent with an enlarged liver. A hard irregular liver with weight loss is a suspected cancer presentation: arrange urgent imaging and a suspected cancer pathway referral.

The findings raise concern for malignancy, including metastases or primary liver cancer, but examination does not establish a tissue diagnosis. Arrange urgent imaging and referral without waiting for tumour markers. AFP and CEA are not universal diagnostic screening tests. Do not biopsy an unexplained lesion before specialist imaging review, particularly when vascular lesions or hepatocellular carcinoma are possible. Use consent and a chaperone for any intimate examination.
THINK: Hard irregular liver and weight loss: metastases.
SAY: "A hard irregular liver; I'm worried about spread."
DO: Start low; edge; percuss; spleen; nodes; rectal exam.
NUMBERS: Edge 6 cm, weight loss 8 kg (scenario).
TRAP: Saying "big liver" and stopping.
FINISH: Imaging, bloods, suspected cancer pathway.
